facts.quote: A trading plan is your strategy for tactically buying and selling assets like stocks, bonds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and other investments.
facts.claim: A trading plan is your strategy for buying and selling.

facts.quote: In short, trading plans help remove some of the emotion and guesswork from your trading decision-making.
facts.claim: A trading plan takes some of the emotion and guesswork out of trading decisions.

facts.quote: Once you've finalized what investments you want to buy, you have to decide when to buy and sell. In trading terms, these are known as your entry and exit strategies.
facts.claim: Deciding when to buy and sell is called your entry and exit strategy.

facts.quote: It's important to determine this process before you start investing so you aren't making spur-of-the-moment choices based on temporary market peaks or valleys.
facts.claim: Set the process before you trade, so you aren't making spur-of-the-moment choices.

facts.quote: You'll also want to determine what percentage of your investable funds will be devoted to each asset type.
facts.claim: A trading plan also settles how much of your money goes into each kind of asset.

facts.quote: You shouldn't alter a trading plan as a knee-jerk reaction to temporary market events, like when stock prices take a dive.
facts.claim: Don't change a trading plan as a knee-jerk reaction to a market drop.

facts.quote: You may wish to change your trading plan over time. Market conditions, your financial situation, and your financial goals change, and you may want to amend your trading plan to reflect that.
facts.claim: Plans can be amended over time as market conditions and your goals change.

facts.quote: And even if you decide to alter your original plan, make sure you devise a replacement to guide your trading.
facts.claim: If you change your plan, write a replacement to guide your trading.

facts.quote: Professional traders live by maxims, and one of the big ones is "Plan your trade and trade your plan."
facts.claim: A traders' maxim: plan your trade and trade your plan.

facts.quote: A trade boils down to a series of decisions about what to trade, how much to trade, when to enter, and when to exit.
facts.claim: Every trade comes down to four decisions: what, how much, when to enter, when to exit.

facts.quote: A watchlist is a list of securities you're interested in trading because they meet certain criteria.
facts.claim: A watchlist is a list of securities you want to trade because they meet your criteria.

facts.quote: For example, criteria for a bullish stock trade could include: Stocks in an uptrend on a daily stock chart.
facts.claim: One example of a watchlist criterion: stocks in an uptrend on the daily chart.

facts.quote: Determining your entry rules before you buy reduces the guesswork when deciding when to enter a trade.
facts.claim: Setting entry rules before you buy takes the guesswork out of when to enter.

facts.quote: after it shows certain entry signals, such as: A bounce off support or a breakout from resistance. A breakout of a basing pattern on a daily chart. A price that closes above a 200-day simple moving average.
facts.claim: Examples of entry signals include a breakout from a base and a close above the 200-day moving average.

facts.quote: Before placing a trade, you also want to specify when and how you'll close it out.
facts.claim: Decide when and how you'll close the trade before you place it.

facts.quote: creating a trade plan can give you a tool for keeping a cool head as you build and reshape positions when markets are on the move.
facts.claim: A trade plan helps you keep a cool head when markets move.

facts.quote: Closing out the trade isn't the final step; instead, you need to evaluate your results.
facts.claim: After you close a trade, evaluate the result.

facts.quote: Record your trades in a trading journal. Review your activities at the end of the month or quarter, and ask yourself the following questions: Were my entries, stops, and exits performed effectively?
facts.claim: Record trades in a journal and review them, asking whether entries, stops and exits were done well.

facts.quote: Also, track your trading history to calculate your theoretical trade expectancy, meaning your average gain (or loss) per trade.
facts.claim: Expectancy is your average gain or loss per trade, calculated from your trade history.

facts.quote: You can calculate a win/loss ratio by determining the percentage of your trades that have been profitable versus those that haven't.
facts.claim: Schwab uses 'win/loss ratio' for the percentage of your trades that were profitable.

facts.quote: How did your trade perform relative to your trade plan, portfolio size, and a market benchmark like the S&P 500® index (SPX)?
facts.claim: Judge a closed trade against your plan, your portfolio and a benchmark.

facts.quote: Paying attention to your performance and tracking it over time can show you what you're doing that works and help you get better results over time.
facts.claim: Tracking your performance over time shows what works for you.

facts.quote: Disciplined traders take risk management seriously. They plan every trade, keeping notes in a spreadsheet or trading journal
facts.claim: Disciplined traders plan every trade and keep notes in a spreadsheet or trading journal.

facts.quote: Working with a trading plan helps retail and professional traders consider every aspect of a trade before they place it.
facts.claim: A trading plan makes you think through every part of a trade before you place it.

facts.quote: allows users to engage in simulated trading with hypothetical funds using live market data.

facts.claim: Simulated results don't ensure success with real money.

facts.claim: A routine won't stop all losses, but it helps prevent mistakes like chasing unfamiliar stocks.

facts.quote: Then check any economic data out before the open and see how it moves the futures market.

facts.quote: When you arrive at your desk, have a sense of the previous day's activity. Review the charts of major indexes to know what sort of market you're in.
facts.claim: A pre-open step: review the major index charts to know what kind of market you're in.

facts.quote: Peterson recommended spending time paper trading and monitoring how you deal with losses before trying it for real.

facts.claim: A watch list is a list of securities you want to track.

facts.claim: Profit factor is gross profit divided by gross loss.

facts.quote: Payoff Ratio is the system's average percentage profit per trade divided by the average percentage loss per trade.
facts.claim: Payoff ratio is the average percentage profit per trade divided by the average percentage loss per trade.

facts.quote: Win Rate The percentage of simulated strategy trades that generated a profit, as opposed to a breakeven result or a loss.
facts.claim: Win rate is the percentage of trades that made a profit.

facts.quote: The maximum number of consecutive winning and losing trades generated by the strategy, based on the time period selected.
facts.claim: Strategy reports track the longest run of consecutive winning and losing trades.

facts.quote: This is the number of winners divided by the number of winners plus the number of losers. It is easy to say we want more than 50%, but the winning percentage will depend on the strategy.
facts.claim: Win percentage is winners divided by all winners and losers; the right level depends on the strategy.

facts.quote: Some traders like high winning percentages and small profits, while others prefer larger profits and lower winning percentages.
facts.claim: Some traders prefer a high win rate with small profits, others a lower win rate with larger profits.

facts.quote: The total profit ($) from the winners divided by the total losses ($) from the losers.
facts.claim: Profit factor is total profit from winners divided by total loss from losers.

facts.quote: This is like an after the fact reward-to-risk ratio. It tells us how much we made relative to each loss.
facts.claim: Profit factor works like an after-the-fact reward-to-risk ratio.

facts.quote: Anything over 1 shows a profitable trading strategy. A Profit Factor of 2.5 means we made a $2.5 profit for every $1 of loss.
facts.claim: A profit factor over 1 means the strategy made money overall.

facts.quote: We need to know how often the strategy wins and losses, as well as the average win percent relative to the average loss percent.
facts.claim: You need both how often a strategy wins and its average win against its average loss.

facts.quote: Typically, we would like to see more winners than losers and the average gain outpace the average loss.
facts.claim: You want the average gain to outpace the average loss.

facts.quote: This is the number of consecutive losing trades. It is important because it gives us an idea of how much pain we may have to endure.
facts.claim: The longest losing streak shows how much pain a strategy can bring.

facts.quote: There will be losing trades and it is important that we use proper position sizing to insure that we can absorb a string of losses.
facts.claim: Losing trades will come; size so you can absorb a string of them.

facts.quote: The golden cross test from 1991 to 2015 produced just 11 signals, which is not a very big sample size.
facts.claim: 11 signals is not a very big sample.

facts.quote: Past performance does not guarantee future performance.
facts.claim: Past performance doesn't guarantee future performance.

facts.quote: It's common among active traders to think of playbook trades as "setups", as in chart patterns, but this is shortsighted.
facts.claim: Treating a playbook trade as just a chart setup is shortsighted.

facts.quote: When the trader merely views the playbook trade as a set of entry criteria, they leave themselves no guidance for sizing the trade and managing the risk/reward of the position.
facts.claim: A playbook trade also needs rules for sizing and for managing risk and reward.

facts.quote: Just as a quarterback and football team works with a playbook to prepare for games, traders have playbooks of the trading patterns that they have tested and successfully employed.
facts.claim: A trader's playbook holds the patterns they have tested and used successfully.

facts.quote: traders forget to update their playbooks when market conditions change
facts.claim: Traders often forget to update their playbooks when market conditions change.

facts.quote: Only setups that empirically demonstrate profitability become an enduring part of one's playbook. The professional trader is one who sticks to their playbook and tests out new plays before adding them to the playbook.
facts.claim: Only setups that show profit on the evidence stay in the playbook; new plays get tested first.

facts.quote: Cherry-picked examples supporting our inference does not constitute an evidence-basis. Rather, we look back over a meaningful sample and count the times when the pattern has and has not led to expected returns.
facts.claim: Cherry-picked examples aren't evidence; count every time the pattern did and didn't work.

facts.quote: Those subjective hunches are the sources of hypotheses, however, not conclusions
facts.claim: Hunches are where ideas start, not proof.

facts.quote: At the end of the day or week (depending on your frequency of trading), identify your best trade and your worst trade. Then dissect each one
facts.claim: At the end of the day or week, take your best and worst trade and dissect each one.

facts.quote: Your best trades are your role models. By reviewing your best trades, you ground yourself in your best practices.
facts.claim: Reviewing your best trades grounds you in your best practices.

facts.quote: A review should finish with a highly concrete game plan for the next day, week, etc. A review without a plan is merely a look in the rear view mirror.
facts.claim: A review should end with a concrete plan for next time; without one it only looks back.

facts.quote: A good review is an efficient review, targeting our greatest successes and shortcomings on the day or week and then making those the focus on our efforts at improvement.
facts.claim: A good review targets the biggest successes and shortcomings and makes them the focus.

facts.quote: For frequent traders (i.e., those who trade intraday and/or every day), a single grade at the end of the day (A, B, C, D, F) indicates the degree to which the goal was met that day.
facts.claim: A report card gives each goal a single grade, A to F, at the end of the day.

facts.quote: Ideally, these comments should include what was happening in markets (and trading) at the time; what was going on in terms of the trader's thoughts and feelings; and what the trading outcomes were.
facts.claim: Journal notes should cover what the market was doing, your thoughts and feelings, and the outcome.

facts.quote: A process goal for a trader might be to limit losses to a certain number of ticks per trade; an outcome goal might be to make a certain dollar amount per week or month.
facts.claim: A process goal is about how you trade; an outcome goal is a dollar target.

facts.quote: The latter is highly dependent upon market conditions and not entirely within the trader's control. Process goals, alternatively, focus on what the trader can control directly and thus reinforce self-efficacy.
facts.claim: Outcome goals depend on the market; process goals are in your control.

facts.quote: Finally, there is evidence that process goals can be more effective than all-or-none outcome goals.
facts.claim: Process goals can work better than all-or-none outcome goals.

facts.quote: A planned trade is one that is guided consciously, filtered according to a variety of criteria that are designed to provide a positive expectancy. The opposite of a planned trade is an impulsive one
facts.claim: A planned trade is filtered by criteria; the opposite is an impulsive trade.

facts.quote: A good trade is not necessarily a profitable one: even the best planning is fallible.
facts.claim: A good trade is not always a profitable one.

facts.quote: By anticipating a variety of possible market scenarios and how he'd respond to each, Paul helps ensure that he will not be surprised by market developments.
facts.claim: Preparing for several possible scenarios means fewer surprises.

facts.quote: It is very difficult to emotionally overreact to situations that we have anticipated and prepared for.
facts.claim: It's hard to overreact to situations you have anticipated and prepared for.

walkthroughs.title: Before the trade
steps: A trading plan is your rules for buying and selling, written before any money is on the line.
Your watchlist holds the stocks that meet your criteria. Entry and exit rules say when you get in and out.
A routine is the same prep every morning: the data out before the open, the index charts, your list.
None of it stops every loss. It cuts down the impulsive ones.

walkthroughs.title: After the trade
steps: Log every trade in your journal: entry, stop, exit, and what you were thinking and feeling.
Review it against the plan, and finish with a concrete plan for next time.
Your best setups, tested and written down, become your playbook.
Grade how you traded, not what you made. A good trade can lose.

walkthroughs.title: The numbers
steps: Win rate is how often you win. On its own it says little.
Put it next to your average win and average loss. Expectancy combines them: your average result per trade.
Profit factor is gross profit over gross loss. Over 1, the winners paid for the losers.
Judge none of it on a handful of trades. A small sample can fool you.

questions.q: A trading plan is best described as which of these?
choices: Your rules for when to buy and sell
A list of stocks you might trade
A record of trades already made
A forecast of where markets go
questions.answer: Your rules for when to buy and sell
questions.why: Your rules for when to buy and sell. Fidelity calls a trading plan your strategy for buying and selling. Deciding when to buy and sell is your entry and exit strategy. Schwab adds that a plan helps you think through every part of a trade before you place it. It removes some of the emotion and guesswork, not all of it.
questions.lesson_line: Write the rules before the money is on the line.

wrong.A list of stocks you might trade: That's a watchlist. The plan says what you'll do with those names.
wrong.A record of trades already made: That's a trading journal. The plan comes before the trade, the journal after.
wrong.A forecast of where markets go: That's a prediction. Fidelity calls a plan your strategy for buying and selling, not a forecast.

questions.simple: A trading plan is your rules for when to buy and sell, made ahead so emotion and guessing play a smaller part.

questions.q: A sharp drop in the market is a good reason to rewrite your trading plan on the spot.
questions.why: False. Fidelity says not to alter a trading plan as a knee-jerk reaction to a temporary market event, like a sharp fall. That does not mean a plan never changes. Fidelity also says you may amend it over time as market conditions and your goals change. If you do, it says to devise a replacement to guide your trading. Schwab's maxim sums it up: plan your trade and trade your plan.
questions.lesson_line: The plan is built for the hard days. Change it calmly, never as a reaction.
questions.simple: False, because a plan should not be changed in a panic when prices drop, only calmly over time.

deeper.example: Prices fall hard on Monday and your stock hits its stop. The panic move is to scrap the plan that night. The plan move is to take the stop as written, then look at the plan calmly later. If market conditions really have changed, Fidelity says you can amend the plan. Make the new plan before you trade on it.

questions.story: Sunday night you write down which stocks you'll trade and how much you'll risk on each. You also note where you'll get in and where you'll get out.
questions.q: What have you just written?
choices: Trading plan
Trading journal
Watchlist
Post-trade review
questions.why: Trading plan. Schwab says a trade boils down to a series of decisions: what, how much, when to enter and when to exit. You made all of them before the open, so this looks forward. A journal records trades after you make them. A watchlist holds only the names. A post-trade review looks back at a closed trade.
questions.lesson_line: What, how much, in and out. Decide all of it before the bell.

wrong.Trading journal: A journal records trades after you make them. Nothing here has happened yet.
wrong.Watchlist: A watchlist is only the names. You also wrote down size, entries and exits.
wrong.Post-trade review: A review looks back at a closed trade. This looks forward.

questions.simple: It's a trading plan: you decided what to trade, how much, and where to get in and out, all in advance.

questions.q: Your plan says: buy on the day a stock closes back above its 200-day moving average. What kind of rule is that?
choices: An entry rule
An exit rule
A sizing rule
A watchlist rule
questions.why: An entry rule. It sets the moment you buy. Schwab says setting entry rules before you buy reduces the guesswork about when to enter. It lists a close above the 200-day simple moving average as one example of an entry signal. An exit rule says when you sell, and a sizing rule says how much.
questions.lesson_line: Entry rules say when you get in. Exit rules say when you get out.

wrong.An exit rule: Exit rules say when you sell. This one says when you buy.
wrong.A watchlist rule: Watchlist criteria pick the names you follow. This rule picks the day to buy one.
wrong.A sizing rule: Sizing rules say how much. This one says when.

questions.simple: It is an entry rule, because it tells you the day you may buy.

questions.q: Your exit rules should be set before you enter the trade.
questions.why: True. Schwab says to specify when and how you'll close a trade before you place it. Van Tharp calls a predetermined exit, your worst-case risk, a key to trading success.
questions.lesson_line: Know where you're wrong before you get in.

questions.story: Your plan says sell if the stock closes under $40. It closes at $39.60. You decide to give it one more day.
questions.q: What just happened?
choices: You broke your exit rule
You adjusted your plan wisely
You followed your plan
You avoided a false breakdown
questions.why: You broke your exit rule. The plan said sell on a close under $40, and $39.60 is a close under $40. Schwab says to decide when and how you'll close a trade before you place it. Fidelity warns against changing a plan as a knee-jerk reaction to a drop. Holding one more day to dodge the loss is that kind of change.
questions.lesson_line: The exit was decided when you were calm. Honor it when you're not.

wrong.You adjusted your plan wisely: A change made mid-trade, to dodge a loss, is a reaction, not a plan.
wrong.You followed your plan: The plan said sell on a close under $40. You held.
wrong.You avoided a false breakdown: Nobody knows that yet. Your rule said sell on a close under $40, and $39.60 is under it. Schwab says to set your exit before you trade.

questions.simple: You broke your exit rule, because the plan said sell on a close under $40 and you held instead.

deeper.trap: The trap is the small miss. A close at $39.60 feels too close to count, so one more day seems harmless. But the rule never said well under $40. Fidelity says set the process before you trade, so you aren't making spur-of-the-moment choices. Steenbarger calls losing well exiting at a point you rehearsed and accepted.

reasons: house sentence removed: A4 had no house fact (h5 is B27 journaling)

questions.q: Which description fits a watchlist?
choices: Stocks you're tracking to trade
Stocks you already own right now
Today's biggest gainers by percent
Your rules for buying a stock
questions.why: Stocks you're tracking to trade. Schwab defines a watchlist as a list of securities you're interested in trading because they meet certain criteria. Fidelity: a list of securities you want to track. It is not what you already own, which are your positions. It is not a list of today's movers, and it is not your rules for buying.
questions.lesson_line: Your list comes from your criteria, not from whatever is moving today.

wrong.Stocks you already own right now: Those are your positions. A watchlist is names you're waiting on.
wrong.Today's biggest gainers by percent: That's a movers list. A watchlist is built from your own criteria.
wrong.Your rules for buying a stock: Those are entry rules. They say when to buy a name on the list.

questions.simple: A watchlist is the stocks you are tracking to maybe trade, picked because they meet your criteria.

questions.story: Each weekend you screen for stocks in an uptrend on the daily chart. The ones that pass go on a short list you check every morning for an entry.
questions.q: What is that short list?
choices: Watchlist
Playbook
Trading journal
Report card
questions.why: Watchlist. It holds names that meet your criteria while you wait for an entry signal. Schwab defines a watchlist as securities you're interested in trading because they meet certain criteria. Its own example of a criterion is an uptrend on the daily chart. A playbook holds setups, a journal holds trades already made, and a report card grades how you traded.
questions.lesson_line: Screen on the weekend. Watch for entries during the week.

wrong.Playbook: A playbook holds your setups, the trades you know how to run. The list holds the stocks.
wrong.Trading journal: A journal records trades you've made. These are trades you haven't made yet.
wrong.Report card: A report card grades how you traded. It isn't a list of stocks.

questions.simple: It is a watchlist, because it holds the stocks that passed your screen while you wait for an entry.

questions.q: What is a pre-market routine?
choices: The same prep steps before each open
Trading before the open
Your trade review after the close
Your rules for how much to buy
questions.answer: The same prep steps before each open
questions.why: The same prep steps before each open. Schwab's veteran traders check any economic data out before the open. They also review the major index charts to know what sort of market they're in. A routine can't stop every loss, but it helps prevent mistakes like chasing unfamiliar names. It is prep, not pre-market trading, and it comes before the open, not after the close.
questions.lesson_line: Same steps, same order, every morning. Then you're ready when the bell rings.

wrong.Trading before the open: That's pre-market trading, a session. The routine is your prep, not your trades.
wrong.Your trade review after the close: That's a review. The routine comes before the open.
wrong.Your rules for how much to buy: That's position sizing, part of your plan.

questions.simple: A pre-market routine is the same prep you do before each open, like checking economic data and the index charts.

questions.q: A good daily routine keeps you from losing money.
questions.why: False. Schwab says having a routine doesn't make you immune from losing money. What it does is help prevent mistakes. Schwab's examples: chasing parts of the market you're not familiar with, or trying to do too much at once. Losses still come. Steenbarger: a good trade is not necessarily a profitable one.
questions.lesson_line: A routine cuts the unforced errors. The market still decides the rest.
questions.simple: False, a routine cuts down on mistakes, but it cannot stop the market from handing you losses.

questions.story: The bell rings and you open a list of today's top gainers. A stock you've never followed is up big, and you buy it.
questions.q: Which habit is built to stop this?
choices: A pre-market routine
A wider stop loss
A longer watchlist
A rule to skip the open
questions.why: A pre-market routine. Schwab says a routine helps prevent mistakes like chasing parts of the market you're not familiar with. Doing your prep means you sit down knowing your list. Steenbarger calls the opposite of a planned trade an impulsive one. A wider stop only limits damage after you buy. A longer list doesn't help if you skip the prep that keeps you to it.
questions.lesson_line: A stock you never prepped is a trade you never planned.

wrong.A longer watchlist: More names don't help if you open a movers list instead. The routine is what keeps you to your list.
wrong.A wider stop loss: A stop limits the damage after you're in. It does nothing about the impulse to buy.
wrong.A rule to skip the open: That only moves the impulse later in the day. You'd still buy a stock you never prepared for.

questions.simple: A pre-market routine, because doing your prep first keeps you on stocks you know and off sudden impulse buys.

deeper.counter: A routine is not a shield against losses. Schwab says it doesn't make you immune from losing money. You can do every step, buy a stock from your own list, and still get stopped out. What the routine removes is this kind of trade: an unplanned buy in a name you never studied.

questions.story: Before the open you write three cases for your stock: gap up and hold, gap up and fade, gap down. For each one you note what you'll do.
questions.q: What does this prep mainly give you?
choices: Fewer surprises, calmer decisions
Better odds the stock goes up
No need for a stop on the trade
Knowing which case will happen
questions.why: Fewer surprises, calmer decisions. Steenbarger: anticipating several possible scenarios, and how you'd respond to each, helps ensure you won't be surprised. He adds that it is very difficult to overreact to situations you've anticipated and prepared for. Schwab says a plan helps you keep a cool head when markets move. The prep changes how you act, not what the stock does.
questions.lesson_line: Decide your moves while it's quiet. Then you're only executing when it's loud.

wrong.Better odds the stock goes up: Prep changes how you act, not what the stock does.
wrong.No need for a stop on the trade: Every case still needs its exit. The gap down case is exactly why you have one.
wrong.Knowing which case will happen: Nobody knows that. Steenbarger: even the best planning is fallible. You write several cases because you can't know which one comes.

questions.simple: It gives you fewer surprises and calmer choices, because you already decided what to do in each case.

questions.q: How would you describe a trading journal?
choices: Your own record and notes on each trade
Your broker's monthly account statement
A list of stocks you plan to buy
Your written rules for trade entries
questions.answer: Your own record and notes on each trade
questions.why: Your own record and notes on each trade. Schwab says disciplined traders plan every trade and keep notes in a spreadsheet or trading journal. Steenbarger says the notes should cover what the market was doing, your thoughts and feelings, and the outcome. A broker statement shows fills and balances, not your reasons or how you felt.
questions.lesson_line: If it isn't written down, you can't review it.

wrong.Your broker's monthly account statement: A statement shows fills and balances. It doesn't hold your reasons, your plan or how you felt.
wrong.Your written rules for trade entries: Those belong in your trading plan. The journal records what you actually did.

questions.simple: A trading journal is your own record of each trade, with notes on why you took it and how it went.

questions.q: A journal entry only needs the trade's profit or loss.
questions.why: False. Steenbarger has traders note what was happening in the market, their own thoughts and feelings, and the outcome. Schwab's review asks whether your entries, stops and exits were done well, which a P&L line can't answer. The profit or loss is one line of the entry, not the whole of it.
questions.lesson_line: The P&L is one line. The why, the how and the feeling are the rest.
questions.simple: False, a journal entry also needs what the market did and what you thought and felt, not just the money.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After each trade, log your entry, stop, exit and how you felt in your trading ___.
questions.why: Journal. Schwab says to record your trades in a trading journal and review them. Steenbarger has the notes cover what the market was doing, your thoughts and feelings, and the outcome. A playbook holds your setups, a watchlist holds stocks you might trade, and a backtest runs rules over past data.
questions.lesson_line: Log every trade. A review is only as good as the record behind it.
questions.simple: Journal, because the journal is where you write down each trade and how you felt, to review later.

questions.q: In trading, what is a playbook?
choices: Your tested setups, written down
The day's list of stocks to watch
A log of every trade you made
A broker's guide to order types
questions.why: Your tested setups, written down. Steenbarger compares it to a football team's playbook: a trader's holds the patterns they have tested and used successfully. Only setups that show profit on the evidence stay in it, and new plays get tested before they are added. Bellafiore builds his by archiving a best setup after each session. A watchlist holds names, and a journal logs every trade.
questions.lesson_line: Your playbook holds the trades you have tested and know how to run.

wrong.The day's list of stocks to watch: That's a watchlist. The playbook holds the setups you trade and how you run them.
wrong.A log of every trade you made: That's a journal. The playbook keeps only the plays worth repeating.
wrong.A broker's guide to order types: Order types are how you send a trade. The playbook is what you trade and why.

questions.simple: A playbook is the setups you have tested and know how to trade, written down.

questions.q: A playbook trade needs sizing and risk rules as well as an entry.
questions.why: True. Steenbarger calls it shortsighted to treat playbook trades as just chart setups. Seeing a play only as entry criteria leaves you no guidance for sizing the trade or managing its risk and reward. Bellafiore reverse engineers the variables of each best trade he archives. Our own rulebook plans every trade as Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail, Advance.
questions.lesson_line: A setup with no size, stop or exit isn't a play yet. It's half of one.
questions.simple: True, because an entry alone gives you no guide for how much to buy or how to manage the risk.

deeper.trap: Many traders save a chart pattern and call it a play. Steenbarger calls that view shortsighted. Entry criteria alone leave you no guidance for sizing the trade or managing its risk and reward.

questions.q: A new setup belongs in your playbook once you've seen it work a couple of times.
questions.why: False. Steenbarger: only setups that empirically demonstrate profitability become an enduring part of a playbook. New plays are tested before they go in. Cherry-picked examples are not evidence. Look back over a meaningful sample and count the times the pattern did and did not work. Van Tharp says even 10 trades isn't a large enough sample. A couple of wins is a hunch, a source of ideas, not a conclusion.
questions.lesson_line: Two good memories aren't a test. Count every time it set up, wins and losses.
questions.simple: False, two wins could be luck, so a setup earns its place only after you test it over many trades.

deeper.trap: The trap is memory. The two times it worked stick, and the times it set up and failed slip away. Steenbarger's fix is to look back over a meaningful sample and count the times the pattern did and did not lead to the expected move. Only a setup that holds up on that count goes in the book.

questions.story: A setup in your playbook worked all year in a steady uptrend. The market turns choppy and the setup fails five times in two weeks.
questions.q: What do you do with the playbook?
choices: Review if it fits this market
Delete the setup for good
Trade it bigger to make it back
Keep trading it the same way
questions.answer: Review if it fits this market
questions.why: Review if it fits this market. Steenbarger sees traders forget to update their playbooks when market conditions change. Fidelity says a plan can be amended over time as market conditions change. Review does not mean delete: a year of evidence may still hold when the market steadies. It also does not mean trading it bigger, or trading on with no check at all.
questions.lesson_line: A play that fits one market can sit out the next. Review it, don't force it.

wrong.Delete the setup for good: A year of evidence doesn't vanish in two weeks. It may just not fit this market.
wrong.Trade it bigger to make it back: StockCharts says to size so you can absorb a string of losses. Raising size into one does the opposite.
wrong.Keep trading it the same way: That ignores the change in the market. Steenbarger sees traders forget to update their playbooks when market conditions change.

questions.simple: Review whether the setup fits this choppy market, because a playbook needs updating when the market changes.

deeper.trap: Two opposite mistakes pull at you here. One is to throw out a setup after a short losing run. Yet even a 60% win rate, which Steenbarger calls quite good, brings several losses in a row many times a year. The other is to keep firing it into a market it was never built for. Steenbarger's answer is review: update the playbook when market conditions change.

reasons: fixed before (wrong note credited a line not on the page)

questions.q: Which one describes a post-trade review?
choices: Grading a closed trade vs. the plan
Checking the news before you buy
Your broker confirming the fill price
Choosing your stop before entry
questions.answer: Grading a closed trade vs. the plan
questions.why: Grading a closed trade against the plan. Schwab says closing out the trade isn't the final step: you need to evaluate your results. Ask how the trade performed relative to your trade plan. Steenbarger adds that a good review targets your biggest successes and shortcomings. Checking news and choosing a stop come before the trade. A fill confirmation is the broker's record, not yours.
questions.lesson_line: The trade isn't over when you sell. It's over when you've reviewed it.

wrong.Checking the news before you buy: That's prep, and it comes before the trade.
wrong.Your broker confirming the fill price: A fill confirmation is the broker's record. The review is yours.
wrong.Choosing your stop before entry: That's part of the plan, set before the trade.

questions.simple: A post-trade review grades a closed trade against your plan, so you learn from it.

questions.q: A review isn't finished until it ends with a plan for next time.
questions.why: True. Steenbarger: a review should finish with a highly concrete game plan for the next day or week. Without a plan, a review is merely a look in the rear view mirror. Bellafiore had his traders send their goals for the next month after reviewing the last one. Listing what went wrong is the middle of a review, not the end.
questions.lesson_line: End every review with what you'll do differently next time.
questions.simple: True, a review ends with a clear plan for next time, or it only looks back.

questions.story: Friday afternoon you pull up your best trade of the week. You go through how you prepared, entered, sized and exited it.
questions.q: Why study your best trade, not only your worst?
choices: It shows what to do more of
It proves the setup has an edge
It's the easiest one to remember
Profit proves you traded it well
questions.answer: It shows what to do more of
questions.why: It shows what to do more of. Steenbarger: your best trades are your role models, and reviewing them grounds you in your best practices. Bellafiore's thesis is to study your best trades and build from them. One trade does not prove a setup has an edge. Its profit alone does not prove it was a good trade either, since good outcomes can come from bad decisions.
questions.lesson_line: Find what you do best, then do more of it.

wrong.It's the easiest one to remember: Ease isn't the reason. The point is to break it down step by step so you can repeat it.
wrong.It proves the setup has an edge: One trade can't show that. Steenbarger counts how often a pattern has and has not worked over a meaningful sample.
wrong.Profit proves you traded it well: That's judging by the result. Annie Duke: good outcomes can result from very bad decisions. Study how you prepared and traded it.

questions.simple: Your best trade shows what you do well, so you can do more of it.

questions.story: Your journal tags every trade by setup. Over three months, one setup lost money on average across its 40 trades. Your other two setups made money.
questions.q: What does your monthly review point you to?
choices: Fix or drop the losing setup
Trade the losing setup more often
Nothing, results by setup are noise
Cut size on all three setups
questions.answer: Fix or drop the losing setup
questions.why: Fix or drop the losing setup. Steenbarger's monthly review breaks P&L down by strategy and trade type. Only setups that show profit on the evidence stay in the playbook. Here one setup lost money on average across its 40 trades while the other two made money. Schwab says tracking your performance over time can show what works. Our rulebook also reviews the numbers each month, like win rate and expectancy. Fixing it means testing the change before you trade it again.
questions.lesson_line: Your journal tells you which setups pay for the others. Act on it.

wrong.Trade the losing setup more often: More of a losing setup is more losses. Build from the setups that work.
wrong.Nothing, results by setup are noise: Breaking results down by setup is what the monthly review is for.
wrong.Cut size on all three setups: The other two setups made money. The review breaks results down by setup so you can act on the one that loses.

questions.simple: Fix or drop the setup that loses, because your review shows it costs money while the other two pay.

deeper.trap: The trap runs both ways. Cutting a setup after a handful of losses can throw away a real edge. Keeping a losing setup because it once worked keeps costing you. Steenbarger's test: look back over a meaningful sample and count the times the pattern has and has not worked, setup by setup.

reasons: fixed before (trade count added to the story)

questions.q: You give your trading a grade, A to F, on each goal you set. What is that called?
choices: Report card
Profit factor
Win rate
Watchlist
questions.why: Report card. For frequent traders, Steenbarger's format gives each goal a single grade, A to F, at the end of the day. He says the daily report card anchors review, goal setting and efforts at improvement. Bellafiore challenged traders to post a report card, not just their P&L. Profit factor and win rate are numbers from your results. They don't grade how you traded.
questions.lesson_line: Grade how you traded, every day. The P&L grades itself.

wrong.Profit factor: That's gross profit over gross loss, a number from your results.
wrong.Win rate: That's how often your trades make money.
wrong.Watchlist: That's your list of names to trade.

questions.simple: It is a report card, because you give each of your goals one grade from A to F.

questions.story: Today you lost money. You took only setups from your plan, sized each one right and sold at every stop.
questions.q: What grade does your report card give your execution?
choices: A high grade, you ran the plan
An F, because the day lost money
Wait for a green day to grade it
A C, good process but a loss
questions.answer: A high grade, you ran the plan
questions.why: A high grade, you ran the plan. Steenbarger's report card gives a single grade, A to F, for the degree to which each goal was met that day. Your goals were about execution, and you met every one. A good trade is not necessarily a profitable one. Bellafiore asks traders to post a report card, not just their P&L.
questions.lesson_line: Clean execution on a red day still earns a good grade.

wrong.An F, because the day lost money: That grades the outcome. The card grades how you traded.
wrong.Wait for a green day to grade it: Steenbarger's card gives a grade at the end of every day. A red day is graded the same way.
wrong.A C, good process but a loss: That blends the P&L back in. The card grades how far each goal was met, and you met them all.

questions.simple: A high grade, because the card grades how well you followed your plan, and you followed it all the way.

deeper.trap: The pull is to blend the two: clean trades but a red day, so a C. That mixes the outcome back into a grade built to keep it out. Grade the execution on its own. The P&L gets its own line, and good execution is the part you can repeat tomorrow.

questions.q: What is a process goal?
choices: A goal for how you trade
A dollar target for the month
A price target for one stock
A goal for your win rate
questions.answer: A goal for how you trade
questions.why: A goal for how you trade. Steenbarger's example: limit your losses to a certain number of ticks per trade. That is in your control. An outcome goal, like a dollar amount per week or month, depends on market conditions. Sport psychologists McCarthy and Gupta say only process goals are fully in your control. A win rate goal is a result, so it is not a process goal.
questions.lesson_line: Set goals you control. Do things well and the outcomes take care of themselves.

wrong.A dollar target for the month: That's an outcome goal. It depends on market conditions you don't control.
wrong.A price target for one stock: That's a trade target. It's about the stock, not about how you trade.
wrong.A goal for your win rate: Win rate is a result. A process goal is the action that leads to results.

questions.simple: A process goal is about how you trade, such as keeping each loss small, which you can control.

questions.story: Your goals this month: 1) Win a trading contest you entered. 2) Never move a stop lower after you enter.
questions.q: Which one is the outcome goal?
choices: Win the trading contest
Never move a stop lower
Both, each one is a target
Neither is an outcome goal
questions.why: Win the trading contest. It is a result, and Steenbarger says outcome goals depend highly on market conditions and are not entirely in your control. Sport psychologists McCarthy and Gupta add that someone else might simply perform better on the day. Never moving a stop lower is a process goal. It is an action you take on every trade, fully in your hands. Only one of the two is an outcome goal.
questions.lesson_line: Outcome goals say what you want. Process goals say what you'll do.

wrong.Never move a stop lower: That's a process goal. It's about how you trade, and it's fully in your hands.
wrong.Both, each one is a target: Only the contest win is a result. The stop rule is a behavior.
wrong.Neither is an outcome goal: Winning depends on the market and on other traders, which you only partly control. That makes it an outcome goal.

questions.simple: Winning the contest is the outcome goal, because it is a result that depends on the market and other traders.

questions.q: Your goals should focus on how you trade, not how much money you'll make.
questions.why: True. Steenbarger: your goals should focus on how you trade, not how much money you'll make. You cannot control the profitability of any single trade. Process goals focus on what you can control directly, while outcome goals depend on market conditions. He adds there is evidence process goals can be more effective than all-or-none outcome goals. Annie Duke says the same: focus on process instead.
questions.lesson_line: You can't control the next trade's result. You can control how you take it.
questions.simple: True, because you control how you trade but not what any single trade pays you.

reasons: fixed before (hedge matched to the source)

questions.q: If a trade loses money, you made a bad decision.
questions.why: False. Steenbarger: a good trade is not necessarily a profitable one. Annie Duke: people make good decisions and still experience bad outcomes. Trading is probabilistic, so losing is part of the odds and you can trade well and lose. SMB even logs losing setups when they were good trades with good risk and reward. Judge the decision by whether it followed the plan.
questions.lesson_line: A clean trade can still lose. Losing is part of the odds.
questions.simple: False, a good decision can still lose money, because losses are part of the odds.

questions.story: Two trades this week. Trade A followed your plan and stopped out for 1R. Trade B was a tip you bought with no stop, and it made three times what A lost.
questions.q: Which trade do you want more of?
choices: Trade A
Trade B
Both
Neither
questions.why: Trade A. It was a planned trade that lost. Trade B was impulsive and happened to win. Annie Duke: people make good decisions and experience bad outcomes, and good outcomes can result from very bad decisions. Judging a decision by its outcome is the trap she calls resulting. Steenbarger agrees that a good trade is not necessarily a profitable one. Our rulebook says never take a trade from an alert or a post without your own entry, stop and size. Repeat the process, not the payout.
questions.lesson_line: Repeat the decisions you'd make again, whatever they paid this week.

wrong.Trade B: That's judging by the result. No plan and no stop is not a habit to build.
wrong.Both: Trade B had no plan and no stop. Duke: good outcomes can result from very bad decisions.
wrong.Neither: Trade A followed your plan. Steenbarger: a good trade is not necessarily a profitable one.

questions.simple: Trade A, because it followed your plan, and a good decision can still lose while a bad one can win.

deeper.trap: Trade B feels better because it paid more. That is the pull Duke warns about: resulting can make you repeat bad decisions and drop good ones. A trade with no stop also had no planned worst case. Tharp says your exit, your worst-case risk, is set before you enter. The big loss Trade B risked just didn't show up this time.

reasons: fixed before (story: a trade with no stop has no R)

questions.story: You risked twice the amount your plan allows on one trade. It ran, and you sold for a big gain. You decide bigger bets pay.
questions.q: What is that mistake called?
choices: Resulting
Curve fitting
Revenge trading
Confirmation bias
questions.why: Resulting. You judged the decision by how it turned out. Annie Duke: resulting is creating too tight a relationship between the quality of the outcome and the quality of the decision. It can make us believe some bad decisions should be reinforced. Breaking your plan was a bad decision that happened to win. The win doesn't make it good.
questions.lesson_line: A win doesn't make the decision good. Grade the decision, then the result.

wrong.Curve fitting: Steenbarger warns against curve-fitting historical tests. Here there was no test, just one live trade judged by its result.
wrong.Revenge trading: Nothing in the story follows a loss. A win shaped your belief, and judging a decision by its result is resulting.
wrong.Confirmation bias: The belief came from the win itself. Judging a decision by how it turned out is what Duke calls resulting.

questions.simple: Resulting, because you judged a bad decision as good just because it made money this one time.

deeper.counter: Flip the story. If the same oversized bet had handed you a big loss, you'd call it a mistake. Same decision, different luck. When your verdict flips with the result, you are grading the luck, not the decision. Duke's point is that a good decision can lose and a bad one can win.

questions.q: What does resulting mean?
choices: Judging a decision by its outcome
Reviewing your results each month
Taking profit at your target
Reporting trades to your broker
questions.answer: Judging a decision by its outcome
questions.why: Judging a decision by its outcome. Annie Duke brought the word from poker. It means creating too tight a relationship between the quality of the outcome and the quality of the decision. Good decisions can have bad outcomes, and bad decisions can have good ones, so one result can't grade the decision. A monthly review of results is a good habit, not resulting.
questions.lesson_line: Good decisions can lose. Bad ones can win. One result doesn't grade the decision.

wrong.Reviewing your results each month: That's a monthly review, a good habit. Resulting is a mistake.
wrong.Taking profit at your target: That's an exit. Resulting is about how you judge a decision afterward.
wrong.Reporting trades to your broker: Your broker records your trades. Resulting is about your own judgment.

questions.simple: Resulting means judging how good a decision was only by how it turned out, which mixes up luck and skill.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Judging a decision's quality by how it turned out is called outcome ___.
questions.why: Bias. Psychologists call it outcome bias: letting the outcome sway how you judge the decision's quality. Annie Duke's poker word for the same trap is resulting.
questions.lesson_line: Outcome bias grades the result and calls it the decision.

questions.q: One losing trade is enough to show your setup doesn't work.
questions.why: False. Annie Duke: you can't use outcome quality as a perfect signal of decision quality, not with a small sample size. One loss is a sample of one. Steenbarger: losing is part of the odds, and you can trade well and lose. Even a sound setup has losing trades.
questions.lesson_line: One trade is a story. Many trades are evidence.
questions.simple: False, one loss is far too few trades to judge a setup, since a sound setup still loses sometimes.

questions.story: You backtest a setup and find 11 trades, 9 of them winners. You plan to double your size on it tomorrow.
questions.q: What's the problem?
choices: The sample is too small to trust
Nothing, most of the trades won
Nothing, if the stop is tight
It needs a higher win rate first
questions.answer: The sample is too small to trust
questions.why: The sample is too small to trust. StockCharts' Arthur Hill calls a test with 11 signals not a very big sample size. Van Tharp says 10 trades isn't enough for expectancy to tell you what to expect over many trades. A high win rate on a few trades can be luck. Past performance does not guarantee future performance.
questions.lesson_line: Trust a long record, not a short lucky run.

wrong.Nothing, most of the trades won: A high win rate on a few trades can be luck. The count is too small to trust.
wrong.Nothing, if the stop is tight: A tight stop limits each loss. It doesn't turn 11 trades into a proven record.
wrong.It needs a higher win rate first: Nine wins in 11 is already high. The problem is the count, not the rate.

questions.simple: The sample is too small to trust, so 9 wins in 11 trades could just be luck.

deeper.trap: Nine wins out of 11 looks like proof. It is the small count Hill warns about, and Van Tharp says even 10 trades isn't enough. Steenbarger wants a meaningful sample, counting every time the pattern did and did not work. Let the record grow before the size does.

questions.q: Which of these describes a premortem?
choices: Picturing the trade failed, then why
Reviewing a trade after it closes
Checking the charts before the open
Testing your setup on past price data
questions.answer: Picturing the trade failed, then why
questions.why: Picturing the trade failed, then why. Gary Klein's premortem in Harvard Business Review: team members assume the project they are planning has just failed. Annie Duke: you imagine failing to reach your goal and ask how that happened. It comes before the trade, unlike a post-trade review.
questions.lesson_line: Before you buy, ask how this one loses. Then plan for it.

wrong.Reviewing a trade after it closes: That's a post-trade review, after the fact. A premortem comes before.
wrong.Testing your setup on past price data: That's a backtest. A premortem imagines a future failure.

questions.simple: A premortem means picturing your trade has already failed, then asking why, before you buy.

questions.story: Before you buy, you imagine it's a month later and this trade was a loss. You write down three ways it could have failed.
questions.q: What did you just run?
choices: Premortem
Post-trade review
Backtest
Report card
questions.why: Premortem. You assumed the trade had already failed, then asked how that happened, before any money was in. Klein's premortem assumes the plan has just failed; Duke applies it to any goal. A review looks back at a closed trade. A backtest runs rules over past data. A report card grades trading already done.
questions.lesson_line: Imagine the loss before the entry, while you can still change the plan.

wrong.Post-trade review: A review looks back at a closed trade. You haven't bought yet.
wrong.Backtest: A backtest runs rules over past data. You imagined a future failure.
wrong.Report card: A report card grades how you traded. Nothing has been traded yet.

questions.simple: It is a premortem, because you pictured the trade already lost and worked out why before buying.

questions.q: What is win rate?
choices: Share of trades that made money
Average gain on your winning trades
Gross profit over gross loss
Number of wins divided by losses
questions.answer: Share of trades that made money
questions.why: Share of trades that made money. StockCharts defines it as the number of winners divided by the number of winners plus the number of losers. Fidelity counts only trades that made a profit as wins, not breakeven ones. Win rate says how often you win, not how much. Wins divided by losses is a different ratio.
questions.lesson_line: Win rate says how often. It says nothing about how much.

wrong.Average gain on your winning trades: That's your average win, a size, not a count.
wrong.Number of wins divided by losses: That compares winners to losers. Win rate puts every trade, winners and losers alike, in the bottom number.

questions.simple: Win rate is the share of your trades that made money, so it tells you how often you win.

deeper.trap: Watch the name win/loss ratio. Schwab uses it for the percentage of your trades that were profitable versus those that weren't. Wins divided by losses is a different number from win rate. Check how a page defines a ratio before you compare numbers. Win rate, as StockCharts defines it, puts winners and losers alike in the bottom number.

questions.q: You made 25 trades: 10 winners and 15 losers. What's your win rate?
questions.why: 40%. StockCharts defines win rate as winners divided by winners plus losers. Here that is 10 winners out of 25 trades, or 40%. The bottom number counts every trade, losers included. Dividing winners by losers gives a different ratio, not a win rate.
questions.lesson_line: Count every trade in the bottom number, losers included.
questions.simple: Your win rate is 40%, because 10 of your 25 trades were winners.

questions.q: Some of the best traders win only about half of their trades.
questions.why: True. Steenbarger notes that many of the Market Wizards claim a win rate not significantly different from 50%. They are hugely successful by keeping losses small. StockCharts agrees the right winning percentage depends on the strategy. Some traders prefer larger profits with lower winning percentages. StockCharts adds that, typically, we'd like the average gain to outpace the average loss.
questions.lesson_line: You don't need to be right most of the time. Keep the losers small.
questions.simple: True, because many top traders win only about half their trades and do well by keeping losses small.

deeper.trap: A 50% win rate sounds like a coin flip, so it's tempting to hunt for setups that win most of the time. The catch is size. The Wizards in Steenbarger's note win about half the time and still do well, because their losses stay small. A high win rate with big losses can still lose money.

questions.story: Trader A wins 70% of her trades. Trader B wins 35% of his. That's all you know.
questions.q: What else do you need to compare their results per trade?
choices: Average win and average loss
Nothing more, A wins more often
How long each one holds a trade
Their longest winning streak
questions.why: Average win and average loss. StockCharts: you need to know how often a strategy wins, as well as its average win relative to its average loss. Schwab calls expectancy your average gain or loss per trade, and win rate alone can't give you that. A 70% win rate with big losses can lose money. A 35% win rate with big wins can make it.
questions.lesson_line: Win rate without the size of wins and losses is half a number.

wrong.How long each one holds a trade: Holding time isn't part of the result per trade. StockCharts pairs how often a strategy wins with its average win against its average loss.
wrong.Their longest winning streak: A streak shows how wins bunch up, not how big each win or loss is.
wrong.Nothing more, A wins more often: If her losses are much bigger than her wins, she can still lose money. Win rate alone ranks nothing.

questions.simple: You need their average win and average loss, because win rate alone says nothing about size.

deeper.example: Picture A winning small and losing big: a few large losses can wipe out many small wins. Picture B winning big and losing small: a few large wins can pay for many small losses. Same win rates as the story, opposite results. That is why StockCharts pairs win rate with average win against average loss.

questions.q: Your three winning trades made $300, $500 and $400. What's your average win?
questions.why: $400. Add up the three winning trades and divide by how many there were. Steenbarger's monthly review tracks average win size next to average loss size. StockCharts: you want the average gain to outpace the average loss.
questions.lesson_line: Average win and average loss are the sizes that give win rate its meaning.
questions.simple: Your average win is $400, because you add the three wins and divide by three.

questions.q: What is the payoff ratio?
choices: Average win divided by average loss
Winning trades divided by losing ones
Gross profit divided by gross loss
Profit divided by account size
questions.answer: Average win divided by average loss
questions.why: Average win divided by average loss. Fidelity defines payoff ratio as the average percentage profit per trade divided by the average percentage loss per trade. TradingView uses the same ratio to measure a strategy's payoff. It uses averages, so it says nothing about how often you win. Gross profit over gross loss uses totals, and that is profit factor.
questions.lesson_line: Payoff ratio says how big your wins are next to your losses.

wrong.Winning trades divided by losing ones: That counts trades. It ignores how much each one made or lost.
wrong.Gross profit divided by gross loss: That's profit factor. It uses totals, not averages.
wrong.Profit divided by account size: That's your return on the account.

questions.simple: Payoff ratio is your average win divided by your average loss, so it shows how big wins are next to losses.

questions.q: Your average win is 6%. Your average loss is 2%. What's your payoff ratio?
questions.why: 3. Fidelity's payoff ratio is the average percentage profit per trade divided by the average percentage loss per trade. Here that is 6% divided by 2%. Your average win is three times your average loss. On its own it doesn't say you make money. StockCharts: you also need to know how often the strategy wins.
questions.lesson_line: Know both sizes. A win rate only means something next to this number.
questions.simple: Your payoff ratio is 3, because your average win of 6% is three times your average loss of 2%.

questions.q: Total profit from all your winners, divided by total loss from all your losers. Which number is that?
choices: Profit factor
Payoff ratio
Win rate
Expectancy
questions.why: Profit factor. Fidelity defines it as gross profit divided by gross loss. StockCharts: total profit from the winners divided by total losses from the losers, like an after-the-fact reward-to-risk ratio. It uses totals. Payoff ratio uses averages, win rate counts winners, and expectancy is the average result per trade.
questions.lesson_line: Profit factor uses totals. Payoff ratio uses averages.

wrong.Payoff ratio: That's average win over average loss, not the totals.
wrong.Win rate: That's the share of trades that made money.
wrong.Expectancy: That's the average result per trade.

questions.simple: Profit factor, because it divides the total won by all your winners by the total lost by all your losers.

questions.q: Your winners made $9,000 in total. Your losers lost $6,000 in total. What's your profit factor?
questions.why: 1.5. Profit factor is gross profit divided by gross loss: $9,000 divided by $6,000. StockCharts says anything over 1 shows a profitable trading strategy. Here the winners made 1.5 times what the losers lost. It uses totals, so it does not tell you how often you won.
questions.lesson_line: Over 1, the winners paid for the losers. Under 1, they didn't.
questions.simple: Your profit factor is 1.5, because your winners made $9,000 and your losers lost $6,000.

questions.q: A profit factor below 1 means the strategy lost money overall.
questions.why: True. Fidelity defines profit factor as gross profit divided by gross loss. Below 1, the gross loss is bigger than the gross profit, so the strategy lost money overall. StockCharts: anything over 1 shows a profitable trading strategy. Exactly 1 means the winners only paid for the losers.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1, the losers outran the winners.
questions.simple: True, below 1 means your losers lost more in total than your winners made.

questions.q: What does expectancy mean?
choices: Your average result per trade
What you'll make on the next trade
How often your trades win
Your largest win so far
questions.why: Your average result per trade. Schwab: your average gain or loss per trade. Van Tharp measures it as the average R-multiple of your trades.
questions.lesson_line: Expectancy is what a trade is worth on average, over many trades.

wrong.What you'll make on the next trade: No single trade is predictable. Expectancy only shows up over many trades.
wrong.How often your trades win: That's win rate. Expectancy also counts how big the wins and losses are.
wrong.Your largest win so far: One big win says little. Expectancy averages all of them.

questions.q: Your win rate is 40%. Your average win is 3R and your average loss is 1R. What's your expectancy per trade, in R?
questions.why: 0.6R. Take 40% of 3R, subtract the losing share of trades times 1R, and you average 0.6R a trade.
questions.lesson_line: Positive expectancy with a 40% win rate. The size of the wins does the work.

questions.q: Win rate 70%. Average win $100. Average loss $400. What's your expectancy per trade, in dollars?
questions.why: -$50 a trade. Schwab defines expectancy as your average gain or loss per trade. You win 70% of the time and still lose $50 a trade on average. The average loss is far bigger than the average win. StockCharts: some traders like high winning percentages and small profits. Here the losses are too big for that style to pay.
questions.lesson_line: A high win rate can still lose money. Check the size of the losses.
questions.simple: You lose $50 a trade on average, because your losses are so big that winning 70% of the time can't cover them.

deeper.trap: A high win rate can feel safe. Here it is 70%, yet one average loss wipes out several average wins. The fix is the size of the loss, not the win rate. Tharp: set a predetermined exit, your worst-case risk, before you enter.

questions.story: Setup X wins 30% of the time, with an average win of 4R and loss of 1R. Setup Y wins 60%, with an average win of 0.5R and loss of 1R.
questions.q: Which setup has the better expectancy?
choices: Setup X, at 0.5R a trade
Setup Y, it wins twice as often
They come out the same
questions.why: Setup X, at 0.5R a trade. It loses more often, but its wins are big. Setup Y wins often, but its wins are small next to its losses, so it loses money on average.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a setup by its expectancy, not its win rate.

wrong.Setup Y, it wins twice as often: Its average win is half its average loss. Winning more often doesn't cover that.
wrong.They come out the same: Work both out. X comes out positive and Y negative.

questions.q: A setup with positive expectancy will make money on the next trade.
questions.why: False. Van Tharp: expectancy tells you what to expect per trade on average over many trades. Steenbarger: even a 60% win rate brings several losses in a row many times a year.
questions.lesson_line: An edge plays out over many trades. Any one of them can lose.

questions.q: You buy at $50 with a stop at $48. You sell at $56. How many R did you make?
questions.why: 3R. Your risk per share was $50 minus $48, the distance to your stop. Your gain was $56 minus $50, three times as much.
questions.lesson_line: Measure every trade in R: the result as a multiple of the risk you took.

questions.story: Your setup has a solid record over 200 trades. Now it has lost four in a row, each one at your planned stop.
questions.q: What does the streak alone tell you?
choices: Losing runs happen to any edge
The setup has stopped working
The next trade is due to win
Your stops are set too tight
questions.answer: Losing runs happen to any edge
questions.why: Losing runs happen to any edge. Steenbarger: a 60% win rate would be quite good. Even so, you will lose several times in a row many times during the year. StockCharts says the longest losing streak shows how much pain to expect. Size so you can absorb a string of losses. Four planned stop-outs after 200 trades don't prove the setup broke. Check whether market conditions changed, but don't judge on the streak alone.
questions.lesson_line: Expect losing streaks. Size so you can sit through them.

wrong.The setup has stopped working: Four losses can come by chance in a sound setup. Check whether conditions changed before you decide.
wrong.The next trade is due to win: A streak doesn't make a win due. Trading is a game of odds, and a 60% win rate still brings several losses in a row.
wrong.Your stops are set too tight: The streak alone can't show that. Each loss hit your planned stop, and even a 60% win rate brings several losses in a row.

questions.simple: It shows losing runs happen to any edge, since even a good setup with a solid record loses several in a row.

deeper.trap: The trap is recency. Four fresh losses feel louder than 200 trades of record, so the setup seems broken. Steenbarger notes a 60% win rate still brings several losses in a row many times a year. The streak is a cue to check your execution and the market, not a verdict on the setup.

questions.q: What is a backtest?
choices: Running a strategy on past data
Trading fake money in a live market
Reviewing your own closed trades
Picturing a trade failed in advance
questions.answer: Running a strategy on past data
questions.why: Running a strategy on past data. The SEC rule describes backtested performance as applying a strategy to past periods when it was not actually used. Those are hypothetical results, not achieved by anyone. Paper trading uses a live market, a review looks at your real trades, and a premortem imagines a failure ahead.
questions.lesson_line: A backtest shows what the rules would have done. Nobody traded it.

wrong.Reviewing your own closed trades: That's a post-trade review of real trades.

questions.simple: A backtest means running your trading rules over past prices to see what they would have done.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Under the SEC's adviser marketing rule, backtested results count as ___ performance.
questions.why: Hypothetical. Under the SEC's marketing rule for investment advisers, hypothetical performance means results not actually achieved by any portfolio of the adviser. Backtested performance is one kind: a strategy applied to past data from a time it was not actually used. The CFTC requires commodity advisers who show simulated results to say they do not represent actual trading.
questions.lesson_line: Backtested results are hypothetical. No account actually earned them.
questions.simple: A backtest counts as hypothetical, because its results were never made in a real account.

reasons: a regulatory rule that can change
fixed before (sentence names the adviser rule)

questions.q: A strong backtest means the strategy will keep working.
questions.why: False. Steenbarger: the future may not mirror the past, and care must be taken not to curve-fit historical tests. The CFTC's required statement on simulated results says no representation is made that any account will achieve similar profits. StockCharts: past performance does not guarantee future performance. A strong backtest is a reason to test further, not a promise.
questions.lesson_line: The past is a guide, not a promise.
questions.simple: False, a backtest shows what worked in the past, and the future may not act the same way.

deeper.trap: A smooth backtest feels like proof. But none of its trades were executed. The CFTC warns such results may misjudge market factors, such as lack of liquidity.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The CFTC's required warning says simulated trading programs are designed with the benefit of ___.
questions.why: Hindsight. The CFTC's advertising rule for commodity pool operators and trading advisors requires a warning about simulated or hypothetical results. It says such programs are designed with the benefit of hindsight. Whoever built the test already knew what prices did, so it is easy to pick rules that fit. That is why the warning also says these results do not represent actual trading.
questions.lesson_line: Every backtest knows the ending. The live market doesn't.
questions.simple: The word is hindsight, because whoever built the test already knew how the past played out.

questions.story: You keep tweaking a strategy's settings until its backtest shows almost no losing years.
questions.q: What's the main problem with this backtest?
choices: Its rules are bent to fit old data
It covers too many years of data
It didn't test enough settings
It needs tighter stops to be safe
questions.answer: Its rules are bent to fit old data
questions.why: Its rules are bent to fit old data. Each tweak you kept made the past look better, so almost no losing years is what you tuned for. Steenbarger warns that care must be taken not to curve-fit historical tests. StockCharts reminds us past results don't guarantee future ones.
questions.lesson_line: Tune a test until it's perfect and you've tuned it to old data.

wrong.It covers too many years of data: More years give the test more trades to judge. The trouble is the tuning, not the amount of data.
wrong.It didn't test enough settings: More settings means more tweaking. Steenbarger warns against curve-fitting historical tests.
wrong.It needs tighter stops to be safe: A tighter stop is one more tweak. The problem is that the rules were tuned to old data.

questions.simple: The problem is that the rules fit old data, not the future, because you tuned them to that data.

deeper.trap: The better a backtest looks after many tweaks, the less it may mean. Each tweak bends the rules toward what the chart already did.

questions.q: Trading with simulated money in a live market, for practice. What's that called?
choices: Paper trading
Backtesting
Swing trading
Day trading
questions.why: Paper trading. Schwab's paper trading tool is simulated trading with hypothetical funds using live market data. IBKR: paper trades won't actually execute on any exchange. A backtest runs rules over past data instead, and swing and day trading are styles, not practice.
questions.lesson_line: Paper trading is practice. It costs nothing, and it proves less than real trades.

wrong.Backtesting: A backtest runs rules over past data. Paper trading happens in today's market.
wrong.Swing trading: That's a style, about how long you hold a trade. It says nothing about practice money.
wrong.Day trading: That's a style too: in and out the same day. Paper trading is about practice money.

questions.simple: Paper trading, because you make practice trades with fake money while the real market moves.

questions.q: Good paper trading results show how you'll do with real money.
questions.why: False. Schwab: simulated performance does not ensure success in a live environment. IBKR: paper trading is not exactly the same as live trading. The CFTC's statement says simulated results do not represent actual trading. Paper is a rehearsal, not the test.
questions.lesson_line: Paper results are a rehearsal. Real money is the real test.
questions.simple: False, paper is only practice, and a good paper record does not mean you will win with real money.

questions.story: A month of paper trading went well. Every order filled at the price you wanted, and losses never bothered you.
questions.q: What should you expect when you go live?
choices: Real fills and real losses differ
The same results as on paper
Live fills usually beat paper fills
Your stock picks get worse live
questions.answer: Real fills and real losses differ
questions.why: Real fills and real losses differ. IBKR's paper fills are simulated from the top of the book, so fills at the price you wanted may not hold live. The CFTC notes simulated results can misjudge market factors such as lack of liquidity. IBKR also calls paper trading financially risk-free. Live, every loss costs real money. In a Schwab article, Peterson says to watch how you handle losses before trading for real.
questions.lesson_line: Paper is risk-free practice. Live, the fills and the losses are real.

wrong.The same results as on paper: IBKR itself says paper trading isn't exactly the same as live trading.
wrong.Live fills usually beat paper fills: Nothing says live fills are better. IBKR's paper fills are simulated from the top of the book, with no deep book access.
wrong.Your stock picks get worse live: Going live doesn't change which stocks pass your rules. What changes is the fill you get, and a loss now costs real money.

questions.simple: Live fills can be worse than paper ones, and real losses cost real money, unlike paper ones.
