questions.q: In our trade plans, what does trim mean?
choices: Take some off at a target
Move the stop up to breakeven
Sell the whole position at once
Add shares as it works
questions.answer: Take some off at a target
questions.why: Take some off at a target. In our plan, trim is where to take some off: a third at 3R, another third at 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Trim into strength at the targets. The rest of the position keeps working.

wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven: That's managing the stop. A trim sells shares.
wrong.Sell the whole position at once: That's a full exit. A trim takes only some off.
wrong.Add shares as it works: That's adding to a winner, the opposite of a trim.

questions.q: In our setup plans, the trims sit at 3R and 5R.
questions.why: True. Our plan sells a third at 3R and another third at 5R. R is your initial risk, entry to stop, so 3R is a gain of three times what you risked.
questions.lesson_line: Trims at 3R and 5R: a third off at three times and five times what you risked.

questions.q: A trading plan settles what to trade, how much, when to get in and when to get out.
questions.why: True. Schwab says a trade boils down to a series of decisions: what to trade, how much, when to enter and when to exit. Fidelity calls when to buy and sell your entry and exit strategies. It says a plan also settles how much of your money goes into each kind of asset. A plan answers all of them before you trade.
questions.lesson_line: A plan decides what, how much, when in and when out, before you trade.
questions.simple: True, because a plan answers what to trade, how much, and when to get in and out.

questions.q: A paper trade does not actually execute on any exchange.
questions.why: True. Interactive Brokers says paper trades happen in a simulated environment. They won't actually execute on any exchange or settle at a clearing house. Fills are simulated from the top of the book, with no deep book access. Schwab's paper trading tool also uses hypothetical funds with live market data. So real fills can differ from paper ones.
questions.lesson_line: Paper fills are simulated, so real fills can differ.
questions.simple: True, because a paper trade is only a practice trade, so it does not go to a real exchange.

questions.q: A profit factor of 2.5 means your winners added up to 2.5 times what your losers lost.
questions.why: True. Profit factor is total profit from winners divided by total loss from losers. StockCharts: a profit factor of 2.5 means $2.5 of profit for every $1 of loss. Anything over 1 shows a profitable strategy. It compares totals, so it says nothing about how often you won.
questions.lesson_line: Profit factor compares money won to money lost. Over 1 means ahead.
questions.simple: True, because a profit factor of 2.5 means your winners made 2.5 dollars for every dollar your losers lost.

questions.q: Outcome bias means letting how a trade turned out sway how you judge the decision.
questions.why: True. Baron and Hershey define outcome bias as taking outcomes into account in a way irrelevant to the true quality of the decision. Annie Duke describes the same trap: judging a decision by its outcome despite the luck in how any decision turns out. It doesn't mean results never matter. Over many trades they are evidence; one result is not.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the decision, not the result. Luck sits in between.
questions.simple: True, outcome bias is when a good or bad result changes how you rate the choice you made.

questions.story: You close a trade on Tuesday afternoon. You plan to write it up in your journal at the end of the month.
questions.q: What does UCT's rulebook say to do?
choices: Write it up the same day
Wait for the monthly review
Write up only the losers
Skip it, the broker logs it
questions.answer: Write it up the same day
questions.why: Write it up the same day. Our rulebook: journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally. Each month we also review the numbers, like win rate and expectancy. Steenbarger's notes cover what the market was doing, your thoughts and feelings, and the outcome. A broker's record holds none of your thoughts.
questions.simple: Write it up the same day, because our rule is to journal every trade the same day.
questions.lesson_line: Ideally, journal each trade the same day and review the week each weekend.

wrong.Wait for the monthly review: The monthly review reads the journal. Our rule is to journal each trade the same day, then review the week every weekend.
wrong.Write up only the losers: Our rule says every trade. Steenbarger calls your best trades your role models, so they belong in the journal too.
wrong.Skip it, the broker logs it: The broker's record has no notes. Steenbarger's notes cover your thoughts and feelings, not just the fill.

Investopedia ('Understanding Trading Win/Loss Ratio', https://www.investopedia.com/terms/w/win-loss-ratio.asp, read 2026-11-09 before the site began refusing the plain client with 402/403) defines it as the number of winning trades divided by the number of losing trades; Schwab's trade-plan page (f16) uses 'win/loss ratio' for the percentage of trades that were profitable (a win rate); many platforms use the phrase for average win divided by average loss. Investopedia's own worked example also mis-states its result (12/18 = 0.67 described as 'losing 67% of the time'; the loss share is 60%). The file never keys 'win/loss ratio': it teaches win rate (Fidelity, StockCharts) and payoff ratio (Fidelity), whose definitions agree, and q38's wrong note only says the name is used more than one way.

Reviewing worst trades: Steenbarger (s11) has traders dissect their best AND worst trade each day or week; Bellafiore (SMB, 2015-04-26, same post as s24) writes 'We do not spend time reviewing our poor trades, ones that were just mistakes or poor risk/reward trades. We discard them.' No question keys whether to review losing or mistaken trades; q22 keys only why the best trade is worth studying, where both agree.
